sections.title: Introduction
sections.body:
> **Audience**: AI engineers building RAG pipelines over PDF / DOCX / TXT corpora where documents contain tables, images, and cross-page references.
> **Companion artifacts**: `notebook_1_tables.ipynb`, `notebook_2_cross_page_references.ipynb`, `notebook_3_images_mixed_content.ipynb`, `notebook_4_page_references.ipynb`.
> **Primary library**: `unstructured` (Unstructured.io) for element-aware parsing, with `chromadb` for the vector store and `sentence-transformers` / OpenAI for embeddings.

sections.title: 1. Introduction & Problem Statement
sections.body:
Most production RAG failures are not embedding failures or LLM failures — they are **chunking failures**. A chunk is the atomic unit a retriever can return, so any information that crosses a chunk boundary is effectively invisible to the system. Three failure modes dominate real-world corpora:

1. **Tables cut mid-row by fixed-size chunkers.** A `RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter` with `chunk_size=1000` sliding over a five-column table will slice through row three. The chunk on the far side of the cut contains cells with no column headers, so the embedding has no idea whether "12,500" is a price, a quantity, or a date.
2. **Tables that span two pages.** Page one ends mid-table; page two continues the table but does **not** reprint the header row. A page-aware chunker that respects page boundaries will produce two fragments, neither of which is self-contained. A page-agnostic chunker will produce one fragment with the page break character stuck in the middle of a row.
3. **Cross-page references in legal and medical documents.** Contracts say "the obligations set forth in Section 4.1 shall survive termination." Medical records say "see lab results dated 2024-03-15." Section 4.1 and the lab results live in chunks N and M respectively. When the retriever returns chunk N, the LLM hallucinates what Section 4.1 says, because the definition is in a chunk the retriever never returned.

This guide and the three accompanying notebooks show how to handle all three scenarios end-to-end, using Unstructured.io for structure-aware parsing and a full RAG pipeline (embedding + ChromaDB + retrieval) to verify the chunking actually works.

sections.title: 2. Why Naive Chunking Breaks on Real Documents
sections.body:
### 2.1 The Table Mid-Row Problem

Consider a pricing table rendered as text:

```
Product | SKU   | Unit Price | Qty | Total
Widget  | W-001 | $12.50     | 100 | $1,250.00
Gadget  | G-002 | $45.00     | 30  | $1,350.00
Gizmo   | Z-003 | $7.25      | 500 | $3,625.00
```

A `RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter` with `chunk_size=80` produces:

- **Chunk A**: `Product | SKU | Unit Price | Qty | Total\nWidget | W-001 | $12.50 | 100 | $1,250.00\nGadget |`
- **Chunk B**: `G-002 | $45.00 | 30 | $1,350.00\nGizmo | Z-003 | $7.25 | 500 | $3,625.00`

Chunk B's first row has no header context. An embedding model encodes "G-002 | $45.00 | 30" as an opaque string; a query like "what is the unit price of Gadget?" retrieves Chunk A (which contains the word "Gadget") but the answer ($45.00) is in Chunk B. The LLM cannot answer.

### 2.2 The Cross-Page Table Problem

The same table rendered in a PDF often spans two pages. Page one shows the header and rows 1–50; page two shows rows 51–100 without re-printing the header. A page-respecting chunker produces:

- **Chunk A (page 1)**: header + rows 1–50 — usable.
- **Chunk B (page 2)**: rows 51–100 with no header — unusable on its own.

If the user asks "what is the unit price of the Gizmo?" and the Gizmo is row 78, the retriever returns Chunk B, which says "Z-003 | $7.25 | 500 | $3,625.00" with no column labels. The LLM cannot answer reliably.

### 2.3 The Cross-Page Reference Problem

A typical contract clause:

> "The license granted under **Section 2.1** shall terminate immediately upon any breach of the confidentiality obligations set forth in **Section 5**."

Section 2.1 (the license grant) and Section 5 (confidentiality) may be 30 pages apart. A 1000-token chunker places this clause in chunk N, the license grant in chunk M, and the confidentiality obligations in chunk P. When the user asks "what happens if I breach confidentiality?", the retriever returns chunk N (which mentions both sections) but neither M nor P. The LLM either refuses to answer or hallucinates the contents of Sections 2.1 and 5.

### 2.4 The ASCII View

```
Document:  [Text...][Title][Text...][TABLE p1][----page break----][TABLE p2][Text...][Section 4.1][Text...]
                                              ^
                                    naive chunker cuts here
                                              |
                                              v
Chunk A: [TABLE p1 partial]          Chunk B: [TABLE p2 no header][Text...]
                                              ^
                                              v
                                    both chunks are useless on their own
```

sections.title: 3. Core Strategy: Structure-Aware Chunking with Unstructured.io
sections.body:
### 3.1 Element-Level Extraction

Unstructured.io does not return a blob of text. It returns a list of **typed elements**, each carrying metadata:

| Element Type     | Meaning                                          |
|------------------|--------------------------------------------------|
| `Title`          | Document title or top-level heading              |
| `Header`         | Section heading                                  |
| `NarrativeText`  | Paragraphs of prose                              |
| `ListItem`       | Bulleted or numbered list items                  |
| `Table`          | A detected table (HTML available in metadata)    |
| `Image`          | An embedded image (crop available on disk)       |
| `Footer` / `Header` | Page furniture (usually noise)               |

Each element carries `.metadata.page_number`, `.metadata.parent_id` (the id of the enclosing Title/Header), and for tables `.metadata.text_as_html`.

### 3.2 hi_res vs fast

- **`strategy="fast"`**: text-layer extraction only. Fast (~1 sec/page) but no table structure detection. Tables come back as raw text.
- **`strategy="hi_res"`**: uses Detectron2 + TableTransformer for layout and table structure. ~3–5 sec/page but tables come back as proper HTML with `<tr>`/`<td>` markup. **Always use hi_res for documents with tables.**

```python
from unstructured.partition.pdf import partition_pdf

elements = partition_pdf(
    filename="contract.pdf",
    strategy="hi_res",
    infer_table_structure=True,            # populates metadata.text_as_html
    extract_image_block_types=["Image", "Table"],  # save crops to disk
    extract_image_block_to_payload=False,  # set True to inline as base64
)
```

### 3.3 `chunk_by_title` — The Workhorse

`chunk_by_title` is Unstructured's semantic chunker. Its rules:

1. Group elements under the most recent `Title` or `Header`.
2. Combine consecutive `NarrativeText` / `ListItem` / `Title` elements into one chunk until `max_characters` is reached.
3. **A `Table` element is never split** — it becomes its own chunk regardless of size.
4. If a section's combined text is below `combine_text_under_n_chars`, it gets merged into the **previous** chunk (avoids tiny orphan chunks under a heading).

```python
from unstructured.chunking.title import chunk_by_title

chunks = chunk_by_title(
    elements,
    max_characters=1500,
    new_after_n_chars=1200,
    combine_text_under_n_chars=300,
)
```

Each returned chunk is a `CompositeElement` (or `Table` / `Image`) with `.text`, `.metadata`, and an `.id`.

sections.title: 4. Scenario 1 — Tables That Span Multiple Pages
sections.body:
### 4.1 Detection

`chunk_by_title` keeps each page's table as a single chunk, but it does **not** automatically merge tables that continue across pages. Detection rule:

> A `Table` element on page N+1 is a **continuation** of a `Table` element on page N if there is no `Title` or `Header` element between them, and either (a) the page-N+1 table has no header row, or (b) the page-N table's caption contains "(continued)" or the page-N+1 table's caption contains "(continued)".

In practice, Unstructured assigns each element a `parent_id`. If the page-N+1 table's `parent_id` equals the page-N table's `parent_id` (same enclosing section) and no Header separates them, treat as continuation.

### 4.2 Merging

Once a continuation is detected:

1. Parse both HTML tables with `pandas.read_html`.
2. If the second table's columns don't match the first, **prepend the first table's header row** to the second.
3. Concatenate the row lists.
4. Re-emit as a single HTML table.

```python
import pandas as pd
from io import StringIO

def merge_cross_page_tables(table_a_html: str, table_b_html: str) -> str:
    df_a = pd.read_html(StringIO(table_a_html))[0]
    df_b = pd.read_html(StringIO(table_b_html))[0]
    if list(df_a.columns) != list(df_b.columns):
        # page B has no real header — assume same schema as A
        df_b.columns = df_a.columns
    merged = pd.concat([df_a, df_b], ignore_index=True)
    return merged.to_html(index=False)
```

### 4.3 Optional LLM Summary for Embedding

Raw HTML tables embed poorly — the markup is noise. A common production pattern is to ask an LLM to produce a one-paragraph natural-language summary of the table, embed the summary, but store the raw HTML for generation:

```python
def summarize_table(html: str, llm) -> str:
    prompt = f"Summarize the following table in 2-3 sentences, preserving key numbers and entity names:\n\n{html}"
    return llm.invoke(prompt).content
```

Store **both** the summary and the raw HTML in chunk metadata. Embed the summary; return the HTML to the LLM at generation time.

See **`notebook_1_tables.ipynb`** for a full end-to-end example including synthetic PDF generation, cross-page table detection, merging, and retrieval verification.

sections.title: 5. Scenario 2 — Cross-Page References in Legal & Medical Docs
sections.body:
### 5.1 The Reference Taxonomy

| Reference Type          | Example                                  | Detection                                  |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------|
| Internal section        | "Section 4.1", "§4.1", "Article III"     | Regex: `(?:Section|§|Article)\s+[\dIVX.]+` |
| Exhibit / Appendix      | "Exhibit B", "Appendix 2"                | Regex: `(?:Exhibit|Appendix|Schedule)\s+[A-Z0-9]+` |
| Defined term            | "the License", "Defined Terms"           | Capitalized phrases listed in a definitions section |
| Date reference (medical)| "see lab results dated 2024-03-15"       | Regex + date parser                        |
| Patient/Case ID         | "Patient #P-1024"                        | Domain-specific regex                      |

### 5.2 Strategy A — Section-Aware Chunking

Split by markdown headers so each chunk carries its section path as metadata:

```python
from langchain_text_splitters import MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter

headers_to_split_on = [
    ("#", "Section_H1"),
    ("##", "Section_H2"),
    ("###", "Section_H3"),
]
splitter = MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter(headers_to_split_on)
chunks = splitter.split_text(markdown_text)
# Each chunk.metadata = {"Section_H1": "4", "Section_H2": "4.1", "Section_H3": ""}
```

For PDFs/DOCX where you don't have markdown, use Unstructured's `Title`/`Header` elements to **reconstruct** markdown before splitting — write `#` for `Title`, `##` for `Header`, etc.

### 5.3 Strategy B — Reference Graph + Parent-Child Retrieval

After chunking:

1. Scan every chunk for references using the regexes above.
2. Build a graph: `chunk_id -> [referenced_chunk_ids]`.
3. At retrieval time, when the retriever returns chunk N, also pull the chunks that N references (one hop).
4. Use LangChain's `ParentDocumentRetriever` or LlamaIndex's `HierarchicalNodeParser` to manage the parent-child relationship: small chunks for precise embedding match, parent section returned to the LLM.

```python
import re

SECTION_REF = re.compile(r"(?:Section|§)\s+([\dIVX.]+)")

def build_reference_graph(chunks: list) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
    section_to_chunk = {}
    for c in chunks:
        path = c.metadata.get("Section_H2") or c.metadata.get("Section_H1")
        if path:
            section_to_chunk[path] = c.id
    graph = {}
    for c in chunks:
        refs = SECTION_REF.findall(c.text)
        graph[c.id] = [section_to_chunk[r] for r in refs if r in section_to_chunk]
    return graph
```

### 5.4 Strategy C — Definitions Injection

Legal documents usually have a "Definitions" section listing defined terms. Extract these once, store them as a separate small collection, and **prepend** the relevant definitions to any retrieved chunk that uses the term. This avoids having to retrieve the definitions chunk every time.

### 5.5 Strategy D — Sliding Window with Section Boundaries

If you must use a fixed-size chunker (e.g., for very long sections), snap chunk boundaries to the next paragraph or section break instead of the next character. This guarantees no paragraph is split mid-sentence.

See **`notebook_2_cross_page_references.ipynb`** for a synthetic 10-section contract with cross-references, the reference graph, and a retrieval test that verifies both the reference and its target are returned.

### 5.6 Strategy E — Page-Level References in PDFs (Page 1 → Page 7)

A particularly nasty variant: the document says **"see page 7"** or **"as described on p. 7"** — a reference by **page number**, not by section. This is common in legal briefs (page cites to exhibits), medical records ("see lab panel on page 7"), and academic papers ("see Methods on p. 12"). The challenges:

1. **PDFs have no section structure** — you cannot fall back to `MarkdownHeaderTextSplitter`. You must rely on the page-number metadata that Unstructured attaches to every element.
2. **Printed page numbers ≠ PDF page indices.** The cover page may be unnumbered, front matter may use roman numerals (i, ii, iii), and the first arabic page "1" may be PDF page 4. You must build a mapping between printed page numbers (what the text says) and PDF page indices (what Unstructured returns in `metadata.page_number`).
3. **References are bidirectional.** When the user asks about content on page 7, you want to also surface the chunk on page 1 that references it — that context often explains *why* page 7 matters.

#### 5.6.1 Detection Patterns

Compile a single regex that captures every common phrasing:

```python
PAGE_REF = re.compile(
    r"(?:see|cf\.?|vide|as (?:described|shown|set forth|stated|detailed) (?:on|in|at)|"
    r"refer to|p\.|pp\.|page|pg\.?|p)\s*"
    r"(?:pp?\.\s*)?(\d+)(?:\s*[-–—]\s*(\d+))?",
    re.IGNORECASE,
)
```

Also catch relative references: "on the next page", "on the following page", "on the previous page", "see overleaf", "see above", "see below". Resolve these to absolute page numbers using the current chunk's page number.

#### 5.6.2 Printed-to-PDF Page Mapping

Most PDFs print a page number on each page (footer or header). After partitioning, for every page, scan the `Footer`/`Header` elements for an integer; build a dict `{printed_page_number: pdf_page_index}`. If a page has no detectable printed number, fall back to assuming printed == pdf index.

```python
def build_page_map(elements) -> dict[int, int]:
    page_map = {}
    for e in elements:
        if type(e).__name__ in ("Footer", "Header"):
            m = re.search(r"\b(\d{1,4})\b", e.text or "")
            if m:
                printed = int(m.group(1))
                pdf_idx = e.metadata.page_number
                page_map[printed] = pdf_idx
    # Fallback: identity for any PDF page not in the map
    return page_map
```

#### 5.6.3 Bidirectional Reference Graph

For each chunk, scan its text for page references. Resolve each printed page number through the page map to a PDF page index, then collect all chunk ids whose `page_number` matches. Build **two** maps:

- `forward[chunk_id] = [target_chunk_ids]` — what this chunk references.
- `backward[chunk_id] = [source_chunk_ids]` — what references this chunk.

#### 5.6.4 Retrieval with Bidirectional Expansion

```python
def retrieve_with_page_refs(query, n=3):
    matched = vector_query(query, n=n)
    expanded = set(matched)
    for cid in matched:
        expanded.update(forward.get(cid, []))   # what this chunk references
        expanded.update(backward.get(cid, []))  # what references this chunk
    return fetch_chunks(list(expanded))
```

When the user asks *"what does the contract say about indemnification?"* and the answer is on PDF page 7, the retriever returns page 7's chunk **plus** the chunk on page 1 that says "indemnification terms are set forth on page 7" — giving the LLM both the definition and the referencing context.

See **`notebook_4_page_references.ipynb`** for a full example with a synthetic 12-page PDF where multiple pages cross-reference each other by page number.

sections.title: 6. Scenario 3 — Mixed Content: Images, Tables, and Text
sections.body:
### 6.1 The Problem

A financial report PDF typically contains:

- Prose paragraphs (financial commentary).
- Bar/line charts (PNG embedded in the page).
- Data tables (HTML-extractable).
- Captions ("Figure 3: Q3 revenue by segment").

If the chunker ignores images, a query like "what was Q3 revenue by segment?" can only match the caption. The actual numbers in the chart are invisible.

### 6.2 The Multimodal Pipeline

```python
elements = partition_pdf(
    filename="report.pdf",
    strategy="hi_res",
    infer_table_structure=True,
    extract_image_block_types=["Image", "Table"],
    extract_image_block_output_dir="./image_blocks",
)
```

Each `Image` element now has `.metadata.image_path` pointing to a cropped PNG on disk.

### 6.3 Generating Text Descriptions for Embedding

Embed the **description**, not the pixels:

```python
from PIL import Image
# Using a VLM (BLIP, LLaVA, GPT-4V, Gemini, etc.)
def describe_image(path: str, vlm) -> str:
    img = Image.open(path)
    return vlm.describe(img)
```

Store the description as the chunk's `.text` (so it gets embedded) and keep `.metadata.image_path` so the original image can be returned to a multimodal LLM at generation time.

### 6.4 Parent-Child for Mixed Elements

A chart, its caption, and the surrounding prose paragraph should be **retrievable together**. Give them a shared `parent_id` (the enclosing `Header`). When any one of them matches, the retriever returns all three.

See **`notebook_3_images_mixed_content.ipynb`** for the full pipeline including VLM description generation, dual-storage (text + image), and multimodal retrieval.

sections.title: 7. Embedding & Vector Store Integration
sections.body:
### 7.1 Chunk Metadata Schema Standardize on this schema across all three scenarios: ```python { "source_file": "contract_2024.pdf", "page_numbers": [3, 4], # list because tables can span pages "section_path": "4 > 4.1", # section-aware chunking "element_type": "Table", # NarrativeText | Table | Image | ... "parent_id": "abc123", # enclosing section chunk id "text_as_html": "...
", # only for Table chunks "image_path": "./image_blocks/3.png", # only for Image chunks "references": ["4.1", "5"], # sections this chunk mentions } ``` ### 7.2 ChromaDB with Metadata Filters ```python import chromadb client = chromadb.PersistentClient(path="./chroma_db") collection = client.create_collection("docs", metadata={"hnsw:space": "cosine"}) collection.add( ids=[c.id for c in chunks], documents=[c.text for c in chunks], metadatas=[c.metadata for c in chunks], embeddings=[embed(c.text) for c in chunks], ) # Filtered retrieval — only Tables results = collection.query( query_texts=["payment terms"], n_results=5, where={"element_type": "Table"}, ) ``` ### 7.3 Parent-Child Retrieval Store two collections: - `child_chunks`: small, precise chunks used for embedding match. - `parent_sections`: large parent sections returned to the LLM. On query, match against `child_chunks`, look up `parent_id`, and return the parent from `parent_sections`. ### 7.4 Evaluating Chunking Quality A chunking strategy is only as good as its retrieval. Build a small eval set: | Query | Expected Chunk Contains | |----------------------------------------------------|-----------------------------------------------| | "What is the unit price of the Gizmo?" | Row with Z-003, $7.25 — across page boundary | | "What happens if confidentiality is breached?" | Both the reference clause AND Section 5 | | "What was Q3 revenue by segment?" | The chart image description AND caption | Measure recall@5. If a query fails, the chunking (not the embedding) is usually the cause.

sections.title: 8. Production Patterns & Pitfalls
sections.body:
1. **Always set `infer_table_structure=True` for PDFs with tables.** Cost is ~3x slower, but accuracy on table queries jumps from ~40% to ~90%.
2. **For DOCX, prefer `partition_docx` over `partition_pdf`.** DOCX has native table structure — no model inference needed, faster and more accurate.
3. **For scanned PDFs, OCR first.** Use `partition_pdf(strategy="hi_res", ocr_languages="eng")` or pre-process with Tesseract. Without OCR, hi_res returns empty elements.
4. **Pin the `unstructured` version.** The library churns fast — `pip install unstructured==0.15.0` (or whatever you tested). Minor version bumps have changed element types and metadata field names.
5. **System dependencies.** Unstructured hi_res needs: `libmagic`, `poppler-utils`, `tesseract-ocr`, `libreoffice` (for DOCX). On Ubuntu: `apt install -y libmagic1 poppler-utils tesseract-ocr libreoffice`.
6. **Build a chunking QA dashboard.** Sample 20 chunks per document class, manually verify: no table is split, no section reference is orphaned, no image is missing its description. This catches regressions before they hit production.
7. **Never throw away raw structure.** When you LLM-summarize a table for embedding, store BOTH the summary (for retrieval) and the raw HTML (for generation). The LLM at generation time needs the actual numbers, not the summary.
8. **Watch chunk size for tables.** A 200-row table becomes a 50KB chunk. Most embedding models cap input at 512 tokens. Either chunk the table by row groups (preserving the header on each) or use the summary-only embedding strategy from §4.3.

| Notebook                                  | Scenario                                              | Synthetic Data Generated                              |
|-------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------|
| `notebook_1_tables.ipynb`                 | Tables, including tables that span two PDF pages      | A 3-page PDF with a 60-row pricing table split p2→p3  |
| `notebook_2_cross_page_references.ipynb`  | Legal/medical docs with section & exhibit references  | A 10-section contract with cross-references           |
| `notebook_3_images_mixed_content.ipynb`   | Mixed content: images + tables + prose                | A 2-page report with a chart, a table, and prose      |
| `notebook_4_page_references.ipynb`        | PDF page-level references ("see page 7") with bidirectional linking | A 12-page legal brief where pages cross-reference each other by page number |

Each notebook is self-contained: it generates its own synthetic input document, runs the chunking pipeline, builds a ChromaDB collection, and runs retrieval tests that **prove** the chunking handles the scenario correctly.

### Prerequisites

```bash
# Python 3.10+
```

sections.title: 10. Quick Reference: Decision Tree
sections.body:
Paste this into your codebase as a `chunking_strategy.py` docstring:

```
def choose_strategy(document):
    if document.has_tables:
        use hi_res + chunk_by_title
        if table.spans_pages:
            apply merge_cross_page_tables()         # §4.2
        if table.row_count > 100:
            embed LLM summary, store raw HTML       # §4.3

    if document.is_legal_or_medical:
        apply section-aware chunking                # §5.2
        build reference_graph                        # §5.3
        use parent-child retriever                   # §5.3

    if document.has_images:
        extract_image_block_types=["Image","Table"] # §6.2
        generate VLM description, embed description # §6.3
        store image_path in metadata                # §6.4

    if document.is_scanned_pdf:
        ocr_languages="eng"                         # §8.3

    # Always
    store metadata schema from §7.1
    build eval set from §7.4
    recall@5 must be > 0.8 before shipping
```

**One-line summary**: Structure-aware chunking beats fixed-size chunking for any document that isn't plain prose. Unstructured.io gives you the element types; the strategies in this guide show you what to do with them.
